newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin vaunts technology edge before Mir repair.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin vaunts technology edge before Mir repair.

text.p: Russian cosmonauts will deploy unique technology to repair the Mir space station, Kremlin officials said on Tuesday, putting a brave face on a run of recent calamities.

"Rumours of the death of the Russian space programme are not only exaggerated but wrong," Yuri Baturin, secretary of the Kremlin Defence Council, was quoted as telling Russian reporters during a visit to the Star City space centre outside Moscow.

"You have to learn to draw advantage from any misfortune. Now, the failure in orbit has forced us to work up an absolutely new and unique technology...No one has this technology yet, but once our crew tries it out, we'll be the only ones," he added.

He gave no details of the innovation. Officials have said they are working on ways to "glue" on an airtight patch to mend a small hole punched in Mir's Spektr module during a collision last month, which cut the station's electricity supply by up to half.

Defence Minister Igor Sergeyev was quoted as saying he was confident the 11-year-old Mir, which brings in vital foreign income for Russia's space industry, would be restored after its worst ever crisis.
"Overall, the crew has faced a record number of mishaps but the crew is carrying out their task, solutions are being found and it looks like all the problems can be sorted out," he said.
Itar-Tass news agency said the two Russians in a relief crew due to blast off on August 5 paid a visit on Tuesday to their launch site at the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.

The two, commander Anatoly Solovyov and flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov, will spend two days inspecting the Soyuz TM-26 spacecraft that will take them into orbit, and checking out the spacesuits they will wear for the repairs.
Around August 18-20, they will don the suits to enter the punctured Spektr module and reconnect the power cables from its solar panels, restoring the lost electricity supply.
Russian space officials decided on Monday to let the new team carry out the repairs and stand down the weary and accident-prone crew now on board.
A Mission Control spokesman said the current trio were getting back to a normal routine after last week's upsets, when one of them accidentally crashed the on-board computer.

The crew were conducting medical and biological experiments. Commander Vasily Tsibliyev, who developed heart trouble after last month's accident, was feeling fine and doing the same amount of work and exercise as his colleagues, the spokesman said.

The two Russians on board will fly home two weeks early on August 14. U.S. astronaut Michael Foale will stay on Mir until September 20, helping out the relief crew but playing no active part in their spacewalks.

Sergeyev, who is drawing up sweeping reforms of Russia's sprawling and underfunded Cold War military machine, said the forthcoming merger of the Military Space Forces with other missile commands would mean more military attention to space.
"The role...of space will naturally grow all the time," he was quoted as saying by Interfax news agency.
